title: Abu Bakr's purchases
hookLine: he spends his wealth buying freedom for enslaved believers, Bilal among them

cards: Abu Bakr is our master, and he freed our master. That's Umar talking, in a report in Bukhari, and the second master is Bilal. We met Bilal earlier this year, pinned under a stone in the Meccan heat, saying only: One.
One. We saw Abu Bakr buy him and set him free. Today the camera turns around, from the man under the stone to the man with the purse, and to the others he paid for.

teach.b: Look at Umar's sentence again. Sayyid, master, is a word for the powerful, and Umar uses it twice. Abu Bakr, the wealthy merchant, is our master.
And Bilal, the man who was bought, is our master too. The voice that called the prayer in Medina had once been property. Bilal was not the only one.
The sirah tells of other enslaved believers, women and men, whom Abu Bakr bought and freed while the Muslims in Mecca were still few and weak. It also tells a small scene at home.
His father, Abu Quhafa, said to him: my son, you are freeing weak people.

teach.h: FREE STRONG MEN, HIS FATHER SAID.
teach.b: If you must free someone, free strong men who could protect you. Abu Bakr answered that he was doing it for the sake of Allah alone. Commentators connect this to verses at the end of Surah al-Layl.

teach.h: ONLY FOR THE FACE OF HIS LORD.
teach.b: In paraphrase: the one who gives his wealth to grow in goodness, who isn't paying back a favor anyone did him, but seeks only the face of his Lord Most High, will be content.
Freeing someone is not a side note in the Qur'an.

teach.h: THE STEEP ROAD: FREEING A NECK.
teach.b: In Surah al-Balad, the steep road a person is told to climb is described as freeing a neck, fakk raqabah, the Qur'an's phrase for releasing a captive or a slave, or feeding someone on a day of hunger.
So when Abu Bakr spent his money, he wasn't buying a name or a bodyguard.
He was buying freedom, and getting nothing back that anyone could count.

how: Islamic law counts freeing a captive or slave as a great good deed and an expiation for some sins, and some Muslims today direct charity toward people trapped in debt or in need of release.

o: bowing the neck low in humble prayer to God
a heavy yoke placed on a defeated enemy
freeing a neck: releasing a captive or slave

games.q: abu bakr's purchases — tap the pairs.

s: abu bakr is our master, and he freed our master.
Abu Bakr chose strong men so they could protect him
his father suggested that; he said he did it for the sake of Allah alone.
freeing a captive appears in the Qur'an's steep road
Surah al-Balad describes it as freeing a neck, or feeding someone on a day of hunger.

games.q: you're Abu Bakr. your father says: you're freeing weak people; free strong men who could protect you. what do you say?
o: good point; I'll buy strong men.
I'm doing it for the sake of Allah alone.
games.why: the sirah has him answer that he did it only for Allah, and commentators link the end of Surah al-Layl to him.

practice: Freedom comes in many sizes: a debt someone can't climb out of, a fee standing between them and a course, a visa, a fresh start, a caregiver who never gets an afternoon off.
Bring one person like that to mind, and settle on something small you could give toward it, with nothing expected back. If you pray, make your intention for the sake of Allah, as Abu Bakr said.

wordCard.voice: Fakk raqabah, 'freeing a neck,' the Qur'an's phrase for releasing a captive, which is what Abu Bakr's money bought, Bilal among them. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: setting a slave free; the act Abu Bakr paid for.

carryVoice: Your line: buying freedom. Two masters in one sentence, and one of them had been bought. Day eight hundred, and still walking.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3754 (Abu Bakr is our master and he freed our master)
